title: Observability: structured logs for collective stalls + scheduler starvation; trace spans around TP collectives
author: Omar El-Sayed
body: Context: As part of the TP stability initiative (ENG-2401 umbrella), we’ve repeatedly struggled to distinguish (a) NCCL/collective stalls, (b) kernel stalls, and (c) scheduler starvation/queueing under mixed workloads. This PR adds structured logs for the two most common “no forward progress” classes we’ve seen in incident triage, and it annotates trace spans around collective calls so we can correlate per-request latency with collective behavior. Motivation: During the 2025-02-13 Sev1 and follow-up escalations (see postmortem + SUP-9827), we had incomplete signals: metrics were coarse, logs were inconsistent, and tracing didn’t include the collective boundary. The end result was slow classification and longer mitigation loops (traffic shift, disabling TP, changing timeouts) than needed. What’s included: 1) Structured logs (JSON) for collective stalls: we emit a rate-limited event when a TP group exceeds a configurable “suspect” latency threshold for collectives (not a hard timeout/abort; those semantics are handled in the watchdog workstream). The event includes enough context to debug without scraping multiple sources: tp_group_id, rank, world_size, collective_type (all_reduce/all_gather/reduce_scatter), dtype, bytes, seq_len_bucket, batch_id, request_id (if available), scheduler_epoch, cuda_stream_id, nccl_comm_hash (non-sensitive), host_id, device_id, runtime_version, and a classification field stall_kind=collective_suspect. 2) Structured logs for scheduler starvation: we emit a rate-limited event when a worker has runnable work but fails to make progress beyond a “starvation” threshold, or when head-of-line blocking is suspected. Fields include scheduler_worker_id, tp_group_id, queue_depth, runnable_count, oldest_enqueue_age_ms, inflight_requests, blocked_on (barrier/collective/kv_cache/mutex), and stall_kind=scheduler_starvation. 3) Trace/span annotations around collectives: we wrap the internal collective call sites with a span (runtime.tp.collective) and attach attributes: tp_group_id, rank, collective_type, bytes, dtype, and a derived attribute collective_suspect=true when it crosses the suspect threshold. We also add a scheduler span event when we log starvation so request traces show “where time went” (queue vs collective). 4) Log safety + overhead controls: logs are behind runtime.enable_tp_stall_structured_logs (default on for Hosted canary, off elsewhere; rollout is handled in ENG-2408) and rate-limited per tp_group_id. We intentionally do not log prompt content; request_id is the internal UUID only. We also ensure we do not allocate on hot paths: formatting is deferred and fields are assembled into a preallocated struct where possible. Implementation notes: - The collective span wrapper sits in runtime/collectives/collective_runner.{cc,h}. We keep the span scope tight (just the actual NCCL launch + wait) to avoid attributing scheduler overhead to collectives. - The “suspect” threshold is read from the existing runtime config plumbing; defaults are conservative (2500ms for suspect logging) and separate from any abort/timeout logic. - Starvation detection hooks into the scheduler tick loop (once per worker per interval) and uses monotonic time; we avoid per-task timers. - Rate limiting is per (tp_group_id, stall_kind) with a token-bucket (burst=2, refill=1/min) to prevent log storms during incidents. Testing: - Added unit tests for (a) log event field presence and (b) rate limiter behavior. - Added a small integration test in the runtime simulator to ensure spans are created and attribute keys are stable. - Manual validation in staging: verified trace shows runtime.tp.collective spans and that logs appear only when thresholds exceeded. Rollout/operations: - This PR intentionally does not add alerts/dashboards; those are in observability-pack PR and ENG-2408. However, the field schema is aligned with the dashboard spec so we can facet by tp_group_id/rank/collective_type. - Oncall note: log signatures are documented in the debugging playbook update (separate doc change) and are meant to quickly classify comm stall vs scheduler starvation without needing GPU-level profiling. Risk: Minimal functional risk; instrumentation-only, with guard flags and rate limiting. Performance risk is mitigated by tight span scopes and no allocations on the hot path; this is also covered by perf-canary in ENG-2409.
commits: runtime/collectives: add trace spans around collective calls and attach TP metadata
runtime/observability: add structured log event schema for collective_suspect + scheduler_starvation
scheduler: add starvation detection hook + rate limited structured events
tests: unit tests for stall logger + rate limiter; simulator test for span creation
docs/comments: document event field schema + config flags
review_thread: Allison Grant (review): Span naming/attributes look good. Two requests: (1) please standardize attribute keys to our tracing conventions (snake_case vs dot notation), and (2) confirm we’re not logging anything that could be considered customer payload. Also, can we make the stall_kind values an enum-like closed set?

Omar El-Sayed (author): Updated attribute keys to follow existing runtime tracing conventions (tp.group_id, tp.rank, collective.type, collective.bytes, etc.) and added a comment documenting the stable schema. Confirmed: no prompt/payload logging; request_id is internal UUID only, and nccl_comm_hash is a non-reversible hash for correlation. stall_kind is now a closed set with compile-time constants.

Sofia Ivanova (review): Starvation detection in worker_loop: can you clarify the condition for “runnable work but no progress”? I’m worried about false positives when a worker is intentionally waiting on a barrier. Also please ensure the log includes blocked_on so oncall can separate barrier wait from scheduler bug.

Omar El-Sayed (author): Good call. I tightened the logic: we only emit starvation when runnable_count>0 AND oldest_enqueue_age_ms>threshold AND worker_state != WAITING_ON_BARRIER, plus we include blocked_on derived from the scheduler state. For barrier waits we emit nothing (the barrier-related logging is handled in ENG-2403/2407).

Hiro Tanaka (review): For the collective span wrapper, are we covering both the async launch and the synchronization/wait? We’ve seen cases where launch is fast but wait hangs. We need the span to include the wait for it to be useful.

Omar El-Sayed (author): Yes—span lifetime wraps the full call (launch + wait). I added an inline comment and split sub-events within the span (event: nccl_launch, event: nccl_wait_begin, event: nccl_wait_end) so we can see where it blocks without changing span boundaries.
Tomáš Novák (review): Rate limiter defaults: 1/min per tp_group_id seems fine, but can we bump burst to 3 for incident forensics? Sometimes first 2 events don’t include the state we care about.

Omar El-Sayed (author): Adjusted burst to 3. Also added a second limiter keyed by (tp_group_id, rank) for collective_suspect so we don’t hide single-rank badness in mixed-rank behavior; still bounded due to per-group limiter.

Aisha Bello (review): Minor: please include runtime_version and region/cluster in the structured event if available; dashboards will need them for correlation. If it’s not available in the runtime process, at least include host_id and let ingestion enrich.
Omar El-Sayed (author): Added runtime_version + host_id always. Region/cluster are not always known in-process; left for ingestion enrichment (confirmed our log pipeline adds cluster/region labels).
Allison Grant (final approval): Approving. Thanks for the attribute normalization + rate limiting; this should materially help our incident classification speed.
Sofia Ivanova (final approval): Approving with the tightened starvation conditions.
release_notes: Runtime now emits rate-limited structured log events for suspected TP collective stalls and scheduler starvation, and adds trace spans around collective execution to improve hang triage and latency attribution.
